syllabus.scope_note: The syllabus marks the final for the last unit, and the past finals (221 A and B) ask about every chapter, so plan for all ten.

style.source: Finals 221 A and B, Majors 181, A, B and C, and Quizzes 222 and 232
question_types: Multiple choice on definitions and scenarios ("which attack is this?")
Matching: scenario to access control model, or attack name to description
Short answers naming and explaining a term (FRR/FAR, degaussing, Biba vs Bell-LaPadula, CRL)
Numeric: RSA keys, encryption and signatures by hand; Diffie-Hellman in the 221 finals
Cipher work: Caesar key finding, Playfair, Vigenère, Hill, transposition, block padding
Correct the false statement (SecSDLC, McCumber Cube, plan types)
Fill a table: asset, threat, vulnerability, STRIDE category, due care vs due diligence
style.note: The 221 finals also asked about Diffie-Hellman, IPsec (ESP/AH) and ARP spoofing, which aren't in the current slides.

chapters.title: Ch 2 · Security foundations, threats and the CIA/AAA principles
Ch 4 · Protection of information assets and governance
Ch 5 · Cryptography: classical ciphers, block ciphers and modes
Ch 6 · Asymmetric cryptography, RSA, hashing and PKI
Ch 7 · Security design principles and models
Ch 8 · Computer and systems architecture security
Ch 9 · ICS/SCADA security for cyber-physical systems

items.name: Defense in depth and the layers of security
items.memorize: Physical, personnel, operations, communications, network and data security, one layer behind another

items.name: Seven critical characteristics of information
items.memorize: Confidentiality, integrity, availability, accuracy, authenticity, utility, possession

items.name: Breach of confidentiality vs breach of possession
items.memorize: A breach of confidentiality always breaks possession; a breach of possession doesn't always break confidentiality (stolen but still encrypted)

items.name: McCumber Cube: three dimensions
items.memorize: Goals: C, I, A · States: storage (at rest), transmission (in transit), processing · Controls: policy, education, technology

items.name: Five components of an information system
items.memorize: Software (hardest to secure), hardware, data (most valuable), people (weakest link), procedures

items.name: SDLC vs SecSDLC phases
items.memorize: Planning, analysis, design, implementation, support · SecSDLC follows the same phases and also identifies specific threats and their controls

items.name: Entities to protect and common protection technology
items.memorize: Endpoints, networks, cloud and data centres · next-gen firewalls, DNS filtering, malware protection, antivirus, email security

items.name: Vulnerability, threat, exploit, attack, control, risk
items.memorize: Vulnerability: a weakness · threat: circumstances that could cause harm · attack: exploiting a vulnerability · control: removes or reduces a vulnerability · risk: a threat plus a vulnerability

items.name: Modern threat landscape and vectors
items.memorize: Supply chain, AI-enabled, cloud and API, insider (intentional, unintentional), hybrid · vectors: malware, ransomware, social engineering, supply chain, APTs, zero-day, AI, IoT/OT, cloud/API

items.name: Malware types, symptoms and countermeasures
items.memorize: Worms, viruses, Trojans, spyware, ransomware (WannaCry, NotPetya) · symptoms: high CPU, slow, crashes, strange files · countermeasures: antivirus, updated definitions, no untrusted attachments, backups

items.name: Social engineering attacks
items.memorize: Phishing · spear phishing/whaling (targeted) · angler phishing (social media) · vishing/smishing · pharming (DNS poisoning) · pretexting · baiting · tailgating · doxing · reverse social engineering

items.name: Social engineering countermeasures
items.memorize: Password policies, physical security, training, operational guidelines, information classification, access privileges, two-factor authentication

items.name: CIA triad: attacks on each and methods to ensure each
items.memorize: Confidentiality: encryption, access control, steganography, 2FA, biometrics, tokens, air gaps (attacks: password theft, port scanning, shoulder surfing, sniffing, privilege escalation) · Integrity: permissions, version control, checksums/hashing, backups · Availability: backups off-site, redundancy, firewalls, WAF (threats: DoS, device failure, disasters)

items.name: AAA services: five elements
items.memorize: Identification (claim) · authentication (prove) · authorization (permissions) · auditing (record events) · accounting/accountability (review logs)

items.name: Protection mechanisms
items.memorize: Layering (defense in depth) · abstraction · data hiding · encryption

items.name: Threat modeling dictionary
items.memorize: Asset, threat (potential event), attack (actual event), vulnerability, threat agent, exploit, control/countermeasure/safeguard

items.name: Risk elements
items.memorize: Threat, vulnerability, asset, damage. Risk = likelihood a threat exploits a vulnerability and harms an asset

items.name: Proactive (defensive) vs reactive (adversarial) threat modeling
items.memorize: Proactive: during design, built in from the start, preferred · Reactive: after deployment or an incident

items.name: Approaches to identifying threats
items.memorize: Asset-, attacker- and software-focused · modern: system/architecture, data, supply chain, environment/deployment, emerging technology

items.name: Three steps of identifying threats
items.memorize: Identify the technologies involved · identify attacks against each element (logical, physical, social) · prevention measures

items.name: Threat models
items.memorize: STRIDE, PASTA (risk-centric), LINDDUN, CVSS, attack trees, Persona non Grata, OCTAVE

items.name: STRIDE: threat, property violated, mitigation
items.memorize: Spoofing → authentication · Tampering → integrity · Repudiation → non-repudiation · Information disclosure → confidentiality · Denial of service → availability · Elevation of privilege → authorization

items.name: Build an asset / threat actor / vulnerability / scenario table
Secure supply chain and assessment methods
items.memorize: All vendors reliable and transparent · assess with on-site visits, document exchange and review, process/policy review, third-party audit

items.name: Information assets: primary vs supporting, and why protect them
Cybersecurity governance vs management
items.memorize: Governance: strategic oversight, "are we doing the right things?" (board, senior leadership) · Management: tactical execution, "are we doing things right?" (CISO, analysts)

items.name: Due care vs due diligence (classify the scenario)
items.memorize: Due care: reasonable protective steps (patches, password policy) · due diligence: investigating and analyzing risks (assessments, auditing vendors). Both avoid negligence

items.name: Government vs commercial classification levels
items.memorize: Government: top secret (exceptionally grave damage), secret (serious), confidential (damage), unclassified · Commercial: restricted/confidential, private/internal, public

items.name: Classification criteria
items.memorize: Business value, legal and regulatory impact, reputational damage, operational impact. "What is the worst impact if this is disclosed, altered or destroyed?"

items.name: PII vs PHI vs proprietary data
Assign sensitivity categories to a list of assets
Protecting data at rest, in transit, in use
items.memorize: At rest: encryption (AES-256), access control, physical and environmental controls · in transit: encrypted channels, secure protocols, monitoring · in use: access control, endpoint security, memory protection

items.name: Data destruction terms, weakest to strongest
items.memorize: Erasing (delete, recoverable) · formatting · clearing (overwrite) · purging (multiple overwrites, degaussing) · destruction (most secure) · declassification. Degaussing doesn't work on SSDs

items.name: Data protection laws: GDPR, US laws, Saudi PDPL
items.memorize: GDPR: EU residents, applies wherever the site is · US: sectoral (CCPA/CPRA, HIPAA for PHI, GLBA for finance) · PDPL: Saudi, since 14 Sep 2023, SDAIA enforces, fines up to SAR 5 million, up to 2 years prison

items.name: Ownership roles: owner, steward, custodian, user, system owner
items.memorize: Owner (department head): classifies, approves access · steward: data quality and business use · custodian (IT): implements technical controls · user: uses per classification · system owner: system security plan (NIST SP 800-18)

items.name: Strategic vs tactical vs operational security plans
items.memorize: Strategic: 3–5 years, why · tactical: ~1 year, what controls (project, hiring, budget plans) · operational: monthly/quarterly, how it runs daily

items.name: Top-down approach and the CISO
items.memorize: Senior management initiates policy and defines acceptable risk; the CISO reports directly to senior management

items.name: Cryptography terminology
items.memorize: Plaintext, ciphertext, cipher, key, encipher, decipher, cryptography, cryptanalysis, cryptology. Cryptography protects confidentiality and integrity, not availability

items.name: Kerckhoffs's principle
items.memorize: The algorithm is public; only the key is secret

items.name: Three dimensions for classifying cryptosystems
items.memorize: Number of keys (symmetric vs asymmetric) · operation (substitution vs transposition) · processing (block vs stream)

items.name: Encryption notation
items.memorize: C = E_K(P) · P = D_K(C) · consistency: D_K(E_K(P)) = P

items.name: Caesar cipher
items.memorize: E(x) = (x + n) mod 26 · D(x) = (x − n) mod 26 (A = 0)

items.name: Caesar and ROT13 encrypt/decrypt (and find the key)
Keyword cipher
items.memorize: Write the keyword without repeats, then the rest of the alphabet in order

items.name: Playfair cipher (5×5 matrix, digram rules)
items.memorize: Pairs: repeated letter → filler X · same row → letter to the right · same column → letter below · otherwise rectangle swap. I/J share a cell. 676 digrams

items.name: Vigenère cipher
items.memorize: Repeat the keyword to the plaintext length; C = (P + K) mod 26, P = (C − K) mod 26

items.name: One-time pad (unbreakable)
items.memorize: Random shift per letter, used once (Mauborgne and Vernam, 1917)

items.name: Hill cipher (matrix mod 26, inverse key)
items.memorize: C = K × P mod 26 per block · decrypt with K⁻¹ (needs the determinant)

items.name: Columnar transposition
items.memorize: Write the text in rows under the key, read columns in key order

items.name: Block count and padding
items.memorize: Blocks = ⌈n / b⌉ · padded bits = blocks × b − n (always pad the last block, unambiguously)

items.name: Block cipher sizes
items.memorize: DES: 64-bit block, 56-bit key (1977) · 3DES: 168-bit · AES: 128-bit block, 128/192/256-bit keys (2001) · IDEA: 128-bit key (PGP) · Blowfish: up to 448-bit · RC5: variable

items.name: Triple DES
items.memorize: C = E_K3(D_K2(E_K1(P))) · P = D_K1(E_K2(D_K3(C))) · K1 = K2 = K3 is plain DES

items.name: Block cipher modes
items.memorize: ECB: C[i] = E(P[i]) · CBC: C[i] = E(C[i−1] ⊕ P[i]), P[i] = C[i−1] ⊕ D(C[i]) · CFB: C[i] = E(C[i−1]) ⊕ P[i] · OFB: V[i] = E(V[i−1]), C = V ⊕ P · CTR: V[i] = E(s + i − 1), parallel

items.name: Cryptanalysis attacks by what the attacker knows
items.memorize: Ciphertext only · known plaintext · chosen plaintext · chosen ciphertext · plus brute force

items.name: Brute force key space
items.memorize: Keys = 2^k (DES 2⁵⁶, AES 2¹²⁸, 3DES 2¹⁶⁸) · substitution: 26! ≈ 4 × 10²⁶

items.name: Symmetric vs asymmetric cryptography
items.memorize: Symmetric: one shared key, fast (~30,000× faster) · asymmetric: public/private pair, trapdoor one-way function, used for confidentiality and authentication

items.name: RSA key generation
items.memorize: n = p × q · φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1) · pick e with gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1 · d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n) · public (e, n), private (d, n)

items.name: RSA encryption and signatures
items.memorize: Encrypt C = M^e mod n, decrypt M = C^d mod n · sign S = M^d mod n, verify M = S^e mod n

items.name: RSA by hand (keys, encrypt, decrypt, sign) with the extended Euclidean algorithm
Hash functions, message digests and collisions
items.memorize: One-way, fixed-length digest, no feasible collisions. Used for passwords and integrity. A collision attack breaks integrity

items.name: Hash algorithm sizes
items.memorize: SHA-1: 160-bit (1993, collisions) · SHA-2: 256/512 (2002) · SHA-3: 224/256/384/512 (2015) · MD2/MD4/MD5: 128-bit (MD4 fast, weaker; MD5 fixes it)

items.name: Hash vs MAC vs digital signature
items.memorize: Hash: integrity, anyone can compute · MAC: hash with a secret key, integrity and authentication · signature: private key, integrity, authentication and non-repudiation

items.name: Digital certificates (X.509 fields) and the certificate life cycle
items.memorize: Version, serial, signature algorithm, issuer, validity, subject, subject public key, IDs, extensions, CA signature · states: in use, revoked, expired

items.name: PKI players: RA, CA, repositories, certificate policy
items.memorize: RA proves identity · CA issues certificates and CRLs (basis of trust) · repositories hold them · CP: what a certificate means

items.name: Public key security services
items.memorize: Privacy, authentication, integrity, non-repudiation

items.name: Security architecture and why design matters
Thirteen security architecture principles
items.memorize: Security by design · simplicity · defense in depth · least privilege · default deny · fail secure · separation of duties · don't trust external systems · zero trust · micro-segmentation · assume breach · continuous monitoring · security automation

items.name: Fail secure vs fail safe
items.memorize: Fail secure: block access, may deny service · fail safe: disable the control, may allow illegitimate access

items.name: Separation of duties: task shadowing vs task splitting
Design and coding flaws, and defences
items.memorize: Maintenance hooks, privileged programs, data diddling, salami (incremental) attacks · defend with trusted recovery and input validation

items.name: Confinement vs process isolation vs bounds
items.memorize: Confinement: read/write only allowed locations (sandbox) · isolation: separate memory and resources · bounds: authority level, user vs kernel

items.name: Security models
items.memorize: TCB, state machine, information flow, noninterference, take-grant, access control matrix, Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality), Biba (integrity), Clark-Wilson, Brewer-Nash (Chinese wall), Goguen-Meseguer, Sutherland, Graham-Denning

items.name: Bell-LaPadula vs Biba read/write rules
items.memorize: Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality): no read up, no write down · Biba (integrity): no read down, no write up

items.name: Access control matrix: ACLs (columns) vs capability lists (rows)
Multitasking, multicore, SMP vs MPP, multithreading
items.memorize: SMP: shared OS and memory · MPP: each processor has its own OS and memory

items.name: Protection rings, operating states and process states
items.memorize: Ring 0 kernel (most privileged) to ring 3 user · supervisory vs problem (user) state · ready, waiting, running, terminated

items.name: Memory types: ROM family and RAM
items.memorize: ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash · RAM: real, cache, registers

items.name: Memory protection mechanisms
items.memorize: MMU and kernel · paging and segmentation · ASLR · DEP · protection keys · process isolation · kernel protection · buffer overflow mitigation

items.name: I/O device protection and firmware (BIOS, UEFI, phlashing)
Client-side vs server-side protection
items.memorize: Client: EDR, browser security (CSP, secure cookies), input sanitization, obfuscation, patching · Server: NGFW and WAF, patching, MFA and RBAC, encryption, IDS/IPS, hardening, DDoS mitigation

items.name: Database threats and best practices
items.memorize: Threats: SQL/NoSQL injection, insiders, misconfiguration, weak encryption, ransomware · practices: least privilege, data masking, encrypted backups, vulnerability scanning, physical security

items.name: Cloud security: models, shared responsibility, threats
items.memorize: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS · hypervisor, elasticity · provider secures "of" the cloud, customer secures "in" it · IAM, CSPM · threats: misconfiguration (top), account hijacking, insecure APIs, insiders

items.name: IoT security challenges and best practices
items.memorize: Weak firmware, no encryption, default credentials, gateway into the network · change defaults, update firmware, segment, zero trust, disable unused features, MFA

items.name: Web threats and mitigations
items.memorize: SQLi → validate input · XSS → escape output · DDoS → mitigation services · broken access control → strict authentication

items.name: Mobile security: device, application, BYOD and its alternatives
items.memorize: Device: full encryption, remote wipe, lockout, screen lock, GPS, app control, storage segmentation · apps: key and credential management, whitelisting · BYOD alternatives: COPE, CYOD, VDI/VMI

items.name: OS protection: technical vs policy mechanisms
items.memorize: Technical: layering, abstraction, data hiding, process isolation, hardware segmentation · Policy: least privilege, separation of duties, accountability

items.name: CPS, ICS and SCADA: definitions and applications
IT vs OT priorities
items.memorize: IT: data, confidentiality first, frequent patching, short life · OT: physical processes, availability and safety first, little downtime, long life

items.name: ICS/SCADA components
items.memorize: Field instruments (sensors, actuators) · PLCs and RTUs · MTU (the heart, initiates communication) · communication network · control centre (OPC server, database, HMI) · SCADA software

items.name: Purdue reference architecture levels
items.memorize: L0 physical process · L1 sensors and actuators · L2 PLCs and RTUs · L3 SCADA and HMI · L4 enterprise IT · L5 cloud and external

items.name: SCADA protocols and ports
items.memorize: Modbus 502 (no encryption or authentication) · DNP 19999, DNP3 20000 (secure authentication) · fieldbus 1089–91 · EtherNet/IP 2222 · EtherCAT 34980 · PROFINET 34962–64 · OPC UA and IEC 61850: high security

items.name: Why ICS/SCADA is vulnerable, and its challenges
items.memorize: No real-time scanning, slow patching, unknown device capabilities, no traffic visibility, weak authentication · cleartext messages, old designs, no patch schemes, scattered remote devices

items.name: ICS/SCADA security objectives in priority order
items.memorize: Availability first, then integrity, then confidentiality · keep running in hard conditions (redundancy) · graceful degradation (normal → emergency → manual) · detect events

items.name: ICS/SCADA security requirements
items.memorize: Protect field instruments (fences, locks, CCTV), protect servers (redundancy, failover, MFA, whitelisting), electronic and physical perimeter (mantrap), network security (NSM, NDR, SIEM), hardening

items.name: ISO 27001 security policies
items.memorize: Clear desk/screen, access control, disposal, data classification, mobile and teleworking, password, penetration testing, backup and recovery, physical security, usage monitoring, third-party access, malware

items.name: Governance, standards and the seven planning phases
items.memorize: Standards: DHS catalog, NERC CIP 002–009, NIST SP 800-82, NISTIR 7628 · phases: assess, document, train, segment, control access, harden, monitor and maintain

items.name: Access, subject, object; identification vs authentication vs authorization
Authentication factors and multi-factor authentication
items.memorize: Knowledge (password, PIN) · ownership (token, smart card) · characteristics (biometrics)

items.name: Biometric errors: Type I (FRR), Type II (FAR), CER
items.memorize: Type I: false rejection · Type II: false acceptance (the one to avoid) · CER: where FRR = FAR; lower CER is more accurate

items.name: Password attacks and one-time passwords
items.memorize: Electronic monitoring, password file access, brute force, dictionary, social engineering · OTP tokens: synchronous (time-based) vs asynchronous (challenge-response)

items.name: Authorization criteria and concepts
items.memorize: Criteria: roles, groups, location, time, transaction types · concepts: authorization creep, default to zero, need to know, ACLs

items.name: Single sign-on: technologies, pros and cons
items.memorize: Kerberos, SESAME, security domains, directory services, dumb terminals · pros: one log-on, stronger passwords, central admin · cons: single point of compromise, legacy systems, implementation

items.name: DAC vs MAC vs RBAC (match the scenario)
items.memorize: DAC: the owner decides · MAC: clearances and labels (military) · RBAC: central roles, best with high turnover

items.name: Access control techniques
items.memorize: Rule-based (firewalls) · constrained interfaces (menus/shells, database views, physical) · access control matrix (capability table per subject, ACL per object)

items.name: Centralized administration: RADIUS vs TACACS+ vs Diameter
items.memorize: RADIUS: UDP, encrypts only the password · TACACS+: TCP, encrypts everything, true AAA · Diameter: builds on RADIUS (RFC 3588) · decentralized: control near the resource, inconsistent

items.name: Accountability: audit review tools, keystroke monitoring, scrubbing
Access control best practices
items.memorize: Deny anonymous accounts, strict access criteria, suspend inactive accounts, replace default passwords, rotate passwords, audit and review, protect audit logs
